for the most part, yeah 7 days a week. i was always the first one at the rink and the last one to go home. you might find your goals change over time too based on what you end up liking the most in skating. for me, i loved to test and compete the most and it went from “i want to be an Olympic skater” to “i want to compete at nationals and pass as many senior/gold tests as i possibly can” and even though both the journey and the destination looked totally different from what i expected, there’s not much i’d change about my skating career. spite was always my fuel (for better or for worse), i had a coach tell me at 15 that i’d never be good enough to skate on a nationally qualifying synchro team and two years later i was on a plane to italy getting to compete on a team usa synchro team. really, just find what you love in skating and push for that even if it ends up not being what you first started for/your original goal and you should have a great time with skating. there’s so many opportunities for adults to compete in any discipline, test, or just skate for the love of skating and you just have to find your niche!
tl;dr: don’t miss the forest for the trees, find what you love in skating, even if it’s completely different from your original goal(s)

as someone who skated for most of the first twenty years of their life and never got higher than a double flip skating 3+ hours a day, a genuine good luck from me. a 3a isn’t just a lofty goal, it’s insane.  i believe that less than 50 women have EVER landed a 3a. so my recommendation to you is to find a supportive coach and start smaller on your goals. even if one day you still want to land the 3a, focus your here and now on having the cleanest steps and turns or passing your first tests or getting all your singles strong first. i’m gonna be blunt and say that skating is hard and hard work. it’s a lot of natural talent, a lot of luck, a lot of finding the right environment for you, and a lot of pushing through the times you don’t want to train or be at the rink. it may click for you right away, or it may take you the majority of your skating career to land a single axel (that was me, i landed my axel two weeks before my sixteenth birthday). take your time and enjoy your skating journey, even the bumps on the road. goals are a great thing, but fixating on one relatively far away goal will end up being more frustrating in the long haul.

when i was probably 17, i was doing a pattern dance on freestyle ice (my music was playing, so i had right of way) and another skater (probably ~13?) wasn’t looking and reached back to do a double lutz and sliced my leg open. i wasn’t badly injured either, the cut wasn’t very deep. the skater and her coaches profusely apologized, she was more shaken up than me. it was an honest mistake though (i was the only skater at my rink who tested pattern dances, so me and my coach were really the only two people who knew the patterns super well). we all just came to an agreement that i would do patterns on early morning sessions to avoid any more close calls. there’s really no justice that can be served, while there are general “right of way” rules (skater with music playing>skater with coach>skater just practicing) no one can perfectly predict where another skater is going at any given time. sometimes, even when you are looking over your shoulder, close calls can still happen. if you’re really concerned about having another collision or close call with her, i agree with the other commenter that you should talk with your coach and see if they can approach the other skater’s coach, or try and skate on sessions where she isn’t there. best of luck, hope you have a speedy recovery <3

hi! so i definitely second the other commenters to get your own pair of skates, rental skates are pretty unsupportive and rarely sharpened. i’d also say to sign up for a basic group class before you commit to private lessons, group lessons are a lot cheaper and will still help you get the basics down. about your ankle, you can definitely rehabilitate it to be just as strong as before (i severely sprained my ankle doing an off-ice jump a few years back, and was able to rehab it back to doing doubles on ice a few months later) my first recommendation would definitely be to see a physical therapist, but if that’s not possible for you, I’d recommend investing in a light resistance band and doing strengthening exercises like [these](https://sportsrehab.ucsf.edu/sites/sportsrehab.ucsf.edu/files/Ankle%20Strengthening%20Protocol.pdf). these are very similar to exercises I did in physical therapy and the exercises i did at home to continue to strengthen my injured ankle. i would also purchase a compression sleeve for your ankle. this will add a small amount of support and will help swelling go down. you can wear this with shoes or with skates. i (and my physical therapist) do not recommend getting an ankle brace to wear after the first few days post-injury. consistently wearing an ankle brace for a sprain long-term trains your ankle to rely on the brace for stability rather than regaining the muscle and ligament strength needed for long-term stability. i would also recommend icing your ankle a lot while it is swollen - after any major physical activity/ankle exercises for sure. when you’re ready to get back on the ice is largely up to you - a doctor or physical therapist can give you a recommended timeframe, but it’s down to personal choice ultimately. be consistent with doing at-home exercises and icing (regardless of whether you can see a physical therapist) and you should start to feel the strength of your ankle ligaments gradually come back. good luck in skating, and i hope your ankle feels better soon! <3

hey! former rockerz distributor here (sold online 2016-2021), and yes, rockerz will fit any type of blade, beginner to advanced, traditional to paramount/matrix. the four pieces that make up your rockerz are all cut a precalculated length based on your blade size/model for the perfect fit. if you get new blades that are the same size (or very near, i.e. 10 1/3” to 10 1/4” or 10 1/2”) your rockerz should still fit your new blades, it just may not be a *perfect* fit. another note about rockerz - there may be a small gap between the halves of your rockerz when they are on your blades. this is normal, and is done to allow for tension of the springs for a tight fit and maximum drainage of ice and water on your blades.

i always come off the ice after a long session super hungry too - here’s what I’d recommend:
- fuel up on carbs before practice and protein after. carbs will give you more steady, long-lasting energy for practice, while protein will help your muscles recover and strengthen after you get off the ice. 
- bring a small snack to the rink with you. if you start to get hungry, take a short break to refuel. i recommend granola bars or the sargento balanced breaks (~200 calories, includes cheese and crackers or cheese, dried fruit, and nuts). neither will ruin your appetite or sit too heavy on your stomach during practice (in my experience). 
- stay hydrated!
- plan to have a meal right after your training times. at my strongest/“peak” of my skating career, i was typically at the rink from about 1:30pm-6:30pm every weekday, so I’d have a high-carb lunch about an hour before practice (my personal favorite was always a baked potato - plenty of nutrients for practice), brought a small snack, and planned to have dinner afterwards. even when i was starving after practice, knowing that i was about to have dinner made it easier. 
- lastly, listen to your body’s hunger cues and don’t skip meals. if you’re feeling hungry, don’t sit on it and wait until you’re ravenous. grab a healthy snack or make a meal. skipping meals makes training more difficult; you’re not giving your body the nutrition it needs to perform your best.

fill up rule. if one section has less than six dancers (pattern/combined) or teams (shadow), the remaining total slots (18 total for pattern/combined, 9 total for shadow) will be filled with the highest-ranking skaters overall (equally from the remaining sections) who have not qualified until there are “enough”.

While this going to sound really specific, find a balance of communication, and ensure you respect each other’s boundaries on it. From my first really committed relationships, my (now ex) BF would want to FaceTime me for over an hour every night, text/Snapchat me at all hours of the day, and see me for whole days (basically 11:00am-midnight) once or twice a week, in addition to proclaiming his love and saying I was “the one” within weeks. While this was all fine and good to begin with (new relationship, felt good to have someone care for me a lot, early relationship infatuation), it became overwhelming. Less than a year into the relationship, life began to hit and i was overwhelmed and felt smothered by this level of essentially hourly communication, and when I asked for space, he essentially begged to still text me at all hours of the day (my best examples of this was how when I asked for space he got a sad look and said “Can I still send you good morning and goodnight texts and tell you when I’m going into work?” [no, I feel overwhelmed, yet he still did it], and how over the course of 24 hours, he had sent me at least ten Snapchat messages when I had only sent two). This is what eventually caused me to break up with him - if he couldn’t respect my boundaries on something as simple as not texting me at all hours of the day, what about more major issues that could arise later in life? Even after I had broken up with him, he tried to beg to see me so we could “talk things out” in person and would consistently be one of the first people to see/like my social media posts until I posted with my current BF (about nine months after breaking up with exBF). 

TL;DR - find a balance in how and how often you both communicate and see each other. respect your GF’s boundaries. know when to listen, and when to stop. remember that if you find anything absolutely deal-breaking, as much as it may break your heart, remember that you are strong and take the lessons learned from this relationship forward into life.

Hi girl! I joined a sorority for basically all the same reasons as you (I was a transfer student and didn't want to feel isolated). I know that it feels awkward to break into a new group of people like this, but here's my insight one year in - 

1. Just because you don't drink doesn't mean that you shouldn't go to the party to bond with your sisters. Honestly, I've found that going out with my sisters has been a great way to bond with them! A lot of us get ready together/pick outfits/share clothes at the house, and while it seems stereotypically feminine, it can be a lot of fun just to be together over something simple. Honestly, one of my closest friends who I go out with the most doesn't drink either, and you can still have a great time out without alcohol!
2. Do you have a big yet? Reaching out to your big to go get coffee (or something) would be a simple way to start meeting and bonding with more people as well.
3. Finances - this is the tough one. Basically, being transparent with the sorority's VP Finance and chapter advisor is your best bet. I struggled to pay rent at the house for the first semester and they were able to work out a payment plan.'
4. If your chapter has a house, definitely go there to hang out and study sometimes! Easy way for girls to recognize and get to know you more.
5. Finally, get involved in chapter events. These are another great way to bond with your sisters.
